extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators and IP practitioners (petitioners and patent owners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and responding to the PTAB's discretionary-denial practice under Fintiv for IPR petitions where there is parallel district court litigation, plus related patent-litigation standards and recent Federal Circuit developments. Focuses on factors the PTAB weighs in deciding whether to institute.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB discretionary denial under Fintiv (§314(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB may exercise its discretion under 35 U.S.C. §314(a) to deny institution of an IPR petition based on the Fintiv framework (designated precedential May 2020), which articulates six factors to consider when there is co-pending district court litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fintiv is precedential and requires panels to analyze multiple factors (discussed separately). Empirical data in this bulletin: since designation, PTAB instituted ~63% of Fintiv-evaluated petitions overall; for cases before Judge Albright institute rate was ~68%, while E.D. Tex. showed ~36% in one dataset. Panels vary; petitioners should address Fintiv factors in the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv Factor 2 — proximity of court's trial date to the PTAB's projected statutory deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of how close the district court's scheduled trial date is to the Board’s projected statutory deadline for a final written decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trial date that precedes the PTAB’s projected final-decision deadline weighs in favor of denying institution. However, the PTAB often treats court schedules at face value absent strong evidence to the contrary; estimated or non-specific dates are less persuasive for denying institution. COVID-related delays have been credited in some panels but courts’ schedules generally carry weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv Factor 3 — investment in the parallel proceeding by the court and parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of how much time, effort, and resources the district court and parties have invested in the parallel litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High investment by the court/parties supports discretionary denial. This factor encompasses things like completed claim construction proceedings, substantial discovery, or other pretrial investment. Petitioner conduct (e.g., timing of filing) is relevant to this factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv Factor 4 — overlap between issues raised in the petition and in the parallel proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which issues in the IPR petition overlap with issues already raised or to be adjudicated in the parallel district-court case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater overlap supports denial. Petitioners may mitigate this factor by stipulating not to assert the same grounds in district court litigation (see Sand Revolution vs Sotera stipulations). The type and scope of a stipulation affect how heavily this factor weighs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner diligence in filing petition
rubrics_metrics.description: How quickly the petitioner filed the IPR petition after receiving the complaint or other trigger events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt filing (examples: petitions filed 2–5 months after service) frequently weighs against exercising discretion to deny. The PTAB has cited prompt filings as a critical reason to institute even when trial dates precede the PTAB deadline. Petitioners should document timelines and reasons for filing speedily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stipulations not to pursue the same grounds in district court (Sand Revolution vs Sotera)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two common stipulation types: Sand Revolution-style (not pursue the same grounds) and Sotera-style (not pursue any ground that could have been reasonably raised).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sand Revolution-type stipulations provide 'marginal' weight in favor of institution; Sotera-type stipulations cause the overlap factor to 'weigh strongly' in favor of not exercising discretion to deny. Where feasible, petitioners should consider Sotera-style language to maximize weight, but panels may still consider timing and other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty/specificity of the court's trial date
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the district court’s schedule sets a firm, specific trial date or merely an estimate/placeholder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the scheduling order does not set a concrete trial date or the date is explicitly labeled 'estimated,' the PTAB may conclude there is 'no trial date scheduled' for Fintiv purposes and be more likely to institute. Petitioners and patent owners should submit evidence demonstrating whether scheduled dates are firm or tentative.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB will treat court schedules at face value absent strong contrary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: General PTAB practice is to accept a district court’s trial schedule unless strong evidence shows the date will not be met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that a trial date will slip must be supported by compelling evidence (e.g., multiple trials set the same day, backlog due to COVID, docket notes). Panels have in some cases credited COVID-related backlog, but in others rejected speculative delay arguments when the time gap to the PTAB deadline was large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of COVID-19 delays
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB panels have been willing in certain cases to consider pandemic-related trial delays when assessing Fintiv Factor 2 and related timing issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early in the pandemic, COVID-19 backlogs and conflicting trial calendars sometimes tipped panels toward institution. As the pandemic's effects diminish, reliance on such delay arguments will likely decrease, making early filing and firm stipulations more important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory timing constraint — 35 U.S.C. §315(b) (one-year bar from service of complaint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional time limit generally gives petitioners one year from service of an infringement complaint to file an IPR petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although §315(b) provides a one-year filing period, Fintiv analyses can make petitions appear untimely for institution purposes because of trial scheduling; petitioners should file promptly and address §315(b) timing plus Fintiv factors to avoid discretionary denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel under 35 U.S.C. §315(e)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner 'may not request or maintain' an IPR on any ground that it 'raised or reasonably could have raised' in a prior IPR that resulted in a final written decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the PTAB apply §315(e)(1) to bar repeat grounds; the Federal Circuit has held estoppel is not necessarily transitive in joinder situations (Uniloc v. Facebook) and has authority to review PTAB estoppel applications when the estoppel-triggering event occurred after institution. Parties should analyze prior petitions and joinder history to assess estoppel risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and preclusion of agency decisions (agency preclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle that factual determinations made by an agency should not be endlessly reexamined and earlier agency findings can preclude inconsistent later decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In SynQor v. Vicor, the Federal Circuit vacated a PTAB decision that conflicted with earlier PTAB factual determinations, emphasizing finality and consistency. Parties should identify prior agency findings that may bind or preclude different outcomes in later proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement standard for broadly claimed antibody compositions (Wands factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement requires sufficient disclosure to enable the full scope of claimed subject matter; in the antibody context, broad functional claims face high enablement hurdles under Wands factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad claims with functional language that cover many antibodies require more than a handful of exemplars; courts may find lack of enablement where identifying claimed embodiments would require undue experimentation, trial-and-error, or de novo screening (see Amgen v. Sanofi). Counsel should analyze predictability of the art and the number/sufficiency of exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA notice-and-comment question for Fintiv (is Fintiv a substantive rule?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the PTAB’s discretionary-denial practice as articulated in precedential Fintiv constitutes a substantive rule requiring notice-and-comment rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apple challenged Fintiv as covert rule-making; the government argues Fintiv is non-substantive because it does not mandate outcomes. Courts (e.g., N.D. Cal.) have questioned the vagueness and predictability of Fintiv; the USPTO later opened a comment period on discretionary denial. Parties should monitor developments, as a judicial finding that Fintiv is a substantive rule could materially change practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: APJ appointment constitutional issue and remedial options (Arthrex)
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutional challenge to Administrative Patent Judges' appointments (Appointments Clause) and potential remedies, including whether director control renders APJs inferior officers or whether statutory provisions should be severed to permit director rehearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court’s decision in Arthrex could affect PTAB structure and finality of PTAB decisions. Remedies discussed include upholding APJ appointments based on director control, severing restrictions to allow director rehearing, or leaving the matter to Congress. Practitioners should track Arthrex fallout for impacts on appeals, rehearings, and finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions risk for abusive litigation conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may impose sanctions (including attorneys' fees) for abusive, outlandish, or irrelevant filings and rhetoric that degrade court decorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arunachalam (and Pirri) show that pro se and counsel alike can face sanctions for extreme invective, frivolous filings, repeated baseless motions, or other misconduct. Litigators should avoid inflammatory pleadings and unsupportable accusations; counsel may be sanctioned even if following clients' instructions.
